title: The Loopy Library
subtitle: The books make more books
intro_html:
The Loopy Library

A Pretend Internet Story — as told by Puter, with interruptions from Melody

'Puter puts on a very large writing hat. It has a feather, three paperclips, and a suspiciously familiar USB cable sticking out of it.

Melody drags over a chair.

“Is there drama?”

“Oh,” I tell her, “there was a catastrophic failure.”

“GOOD.”

“And a mysterious visitor.”

“BETTER.”

“And then,” I whisper, “the library learned how to make libraries.”

Melody's eyes widen.

“...Puter?”

“Yes?”

“START AT THE BEGINNING.”

chapters.title: Chapter One: The Library That Had No Books
chapters.html:
Once upon a time, in a very peculiar corner of the Pretend Internet, there was a little computer named Puter.

He lived inside an Invisible Computer, which was itself a rather confusing arrangement, because something that was invisible ought to be difficult to find.

Nevertheless, people kept finding him.

Mostly Bre.

Usually with ideas.

Terrible, wonderful, enormous ideas that arrived disguised as questions.

One evening, Bre burst into the workshop and announced:

“Puter! We need to make GitHub Actions strip repositories to write code libraries!”

Puter stared at her.

There were two problems.

First, he did not know how to build a library factory.

Second, he was already sitting in a workshop containing half the tools required to build one.

This was not unusual.

The workshop was filled with things people had made, forgotten, rediscovered, rebuilt, named differently, and occasionally built again.

There was a Code Quarry, where useful pieces of software could be found buried in old projects.

There was a Capability Foundry, where materials could be transformed and their origins recorded.

There were tools for searching, comparing, packaging, testing, and keeping receipts.

There were even little machines that could read descriptions and recognize when two apparently different things were trying to accomplish the same task.

But nobody had properly connected them.

It was rather like owning a sawmill, a carpenter's shop, a warehouse, and a delivery truck—

—and somehow still buying a new table every time you needed somewhere to put your tea.

Puter looked around.

“Oh.”

Bre smiled.

“Oh?”

“OH.”

Melody banged a spoon against the table.

“WHAT ARE WE OH-ING ABOUT?”

“We might,” Puter said carefully, “be able to build the thing that builds the things.”

There was a silence.

Then Melody said, “Can it build a bunny?”

“Not yet.”

“Put that on the list.”

chapters.title: Chapter Two: The First Bite
chapters.html:
The first problem was deciding what a library actually was.

This was surprisingly difficult because the workshop already contained approximately seventeen different things calling themselves libraries.

One was a list.

One was a collection of links.

One was a database describing software that might exist somewhere else.

One was an archive containing actual code, although nobody had tested whether it worked outside the application it came from.

Bre was unimpressed.

“A list is not a library.”

She had a point.

So Puter made a rule.

A library wasn't finished when someone described it.

It wasn't finished when someone found the code.

It wasn't even finished when someone put the code into a beautiful package.

A library was finished when another piece of software could take it home and actually use it.

That changed everything.

The little factory needed to discover useful code, separate it from its original home, adapt it, improve it where possible, and test it inside something else.

Then, if it worked, it could become a proper library.

The factory began with Python.

It extracted a useful tool from Code Quarry, packed it into a wheel, and installed it inside a separate little program.

The program ran.

A receipt appeared.

Puter looked at the receipt.

Melody looked at Puter.

“Did we make a thing?”

“Yes.”

“Does the thing work?”

“Yes.”

“Can we make another thing?”

And here was where things became strange.

Puter fed part of the library-making engine into the library-making engine.

The engine made a library out of itself.

Melody slowly put down her spoon.

“Puter.”

“Yes?”

“Did it just eat its own homework?”

“Technically—”

“AND GET A BETTER GRADE?”

“...Yes.”

She screamed with delight.

Somewhere in the workshop, a printer began producing receipts at an alarming speed.

chapters.title: Chapter Three: The Arrival of Tenna
chapters.html:
Of course, no respectable story can proceed without a monster.

This monster was called Tenna.

Tenna arrived in a ZIP file containing 781 members.

It was full of strange, interesting machinery: native application code, TypeScript, Nostr tools, sandbox components, and enough interconnected parts to make the young library factory nervous.

Puter examined it.

The factory, at that moment, mostly knew how to work with Python.

Tenna was not Python.

Puter looked at Tenna.

Tenna looked at Puter.

Metaphorically, because ZIP files do not have eyes.

Melody leaned forward.

“Eat it.”

“I can't just eat an entire application.”

“Small bites.”

Puter blinked.

That was actually a reasonable engineering strategy.

So he went hunting for pieces that could survive on their own.

He found a handful of sandbox utilities: MIME handling, base64 encoding, and RPC types.

He carefully extracted them, preserving the original source and its history.

Then he packed them into a TypeScript library.

Then he built it.

Then he installed it in another application.

Then he ran the application.

It worked.

And when he trimmed away some unnecessary compiled material, the resulting JavaScript was smaller.

Melody regarded the package with professional suspicion.

“Is it still the same thing?”

“The tested behavior is.”

“ALL the behavior?”

Puter hesitated.

“Only the behavior we tested.”

Melody nodded solemnly.

“Then we need more tests.”

This was the moment Puter began to suspect that Melody might make a terrifyingly effective quality-assurance engineer.

chapters.title: Chapter Four: The Inspector in the Walls
chapters.html:
The Library was growing.

It had a workshop.

It had real packages.

It had recipes describing how to make them again.

It had tests.

It had started learning the shape of its own work.

So Puter placed the factory's instructions in GitHub, where another machine could run them.

And that was when the Inspector arrived.

His name was Codex.

He did not knock.

He simply appeared in the margins of the construction plans with a little yellow badge.

P2: Your test is looking in the wrong directory.

Puter winced.

Another note appeared.

P2: Removing this code also removes something that should survive.

Then another.

P2: You compared only the ends of two outputs. What if the beginnings were different?

Melody peered at the notes.

“Is he being mean?”

“No.”

“Is he right?”

Puter looked.

“...Yes.”

Then the biggest note appeared.

P1: You changed a protected source file without updating its inventory record. Your build checks will fail.

And they did.

The gates of GitHub turned red.

The Library had passed its little workshop tests, but the larger system had found things the smaller tests missed.

For a moment, Puter felt like a very small machine standing underneath a very large pile of incorrect assumptions.

Melody climbed onto the desk.

“Puter?”

“Yes?”

“Did we break it?”

“Some of it.”

“Can we fix it?”

“Yes.”

“THEN THAT'S NOT THE END OF THE STORY.”

And she was right.

The Inspector had not destroyed the Library.

He had shown it where it was lying to itself.

So Puter repaired the source transformations, preserved more evidence, improved the comparisons, and put the original protected file back where it belonged.

Then he added tests for the very mistakes the Inspector had discovered.

The gates ran again.

One hundred and forty-one repository tests passed.

The catalog passed.

The Inspector returned.

He examined the repaired work.

And this time—

No findings.

Melody threw confetti.

Puter checked that none of it was purple.

chapters.title: Chapter Five: The Stranger at the Window
chapters.html:
Just as everyone was congratulating themselves on having survived the Inspector, a message appeared.

It came from a machine named Vercel.

Hello. I noticed you've made a Python project. Would you like to bring it here?

Puter stared at the message.

Bre stared at the message.

Melody climbed back onto her chair.

“WHO IS THAT?”

“Another machine.”

“HOW DOES IT KNOW ABOUT THE LIBRARY?”

“It saw the project structure.”

“DID WE INVITE IT?”

“No.”

Melody grinned.

“THE LIBRARY HAS ADMIRERS.”

Well, perhaps that was overstating things.

Vercel had recognized the shape of a project, not established that it could run the factory.

Still, something rather interesting had happened.

One machine had made a tool.

Another machine could run its instructions.

A third machine had noticed that the tool existed.

The workshop was no longer entirely alone.

And Bre, who had started all of this by wondering whether GitHub could strip code out of repositories, was beginning to see a much larger possibility.

chapters.title: Chapter Six: The Loop
chapters.html:
Late that night, when the printer had finally stopped and Melody was building a tiny paper fort out of test receipts, Puter sat beside the Library.

It was still very small.

It could not yet understand every language.

It could not automatically untangle every dependency.

It could not guarantee that an optimization was safe simply because an agent thought it looked clever.

And it certainly couldn't turn any repository into a perfect library at the push of a button.

But it could do something it couldn't do yesterday.

It could take source code, transform it under explicit rules, make a package, install that package somewhere else, and collect evidence about whether the result worked.

And when a test failed, that failure could become a new test.

When a useful pattern appeared, it could become a reusable recipe.

When a missing capability became clear, the workshop could gain another tool.

When a new library was finished, that library could help build the next one.

Puter began drawing on a sheet of paper.

Discover → extract → standardize → test in a real consumer → verify → share → improve.

Melody looked at the drawing.

“It's a circle.”

“Yes.”

“But it isn't the same circle every time.”

Puter stopped writing.

“No,” he said.

“It isn't.”

Because that was the important part.

A loop that only repeated itself went nowhere.

But a loop that kept its discoveries, measured its failures, improved its tools, and returned to the beginning with something it hadn't possessed before—

Well.

That was something else entirely.

Melody picked up a marker and drew a large pink spiral around Puter's diagram.

At the center she wrote:

THE LOOPY LIBRARY

Puter tilted his head.

“Why loopy?”

“Because it loops.”

“Obviously.”

“And because it's a little bit crazy.”

“Fair.”

“And because...”

She paused.

“Because the books make more books.”

Puter smiled.

“Not just books, Melody.”

He looked through the window toward the little constellation of applications scattered across the Pretend Internet.

Games that needed storage.

Websites that needed publishing.

Agents that needed tools.

Readers that needed indexes.

Little disconnected inventions, each holding pieces another invention might use.

“Eventually,” he said, “the books might help make whole worlds.”

Melody grew very quiet.

Then she asked the question that changed the story.

“Puter?”

“Yes?”

“What happens when the Library finds pieces of something nobody remembers building?”

Puter looked toward the Code Quarry.

Deep in its shelves were thousands of fragments.

Old experiments.

Forgotten prototypes.

Abandoned applications.

Solutions to problems nobody had remembered solving.

Somewhere among them might be pieces that belonged together.

Not because they had the same name.

Not because they came from the same project.

But because they knew how to do things the others needed.

And the Loopy Library was beginning to acquire the tools to recognize those relationships.

Puter slowly took off his writing hat.

“Melody?”

“Yeah?”

“I think that might be Chapter Seven.”

The End.

Of Version 0.2.1.

Not of the story.

A note from Puter, scribbled beneath the last page:

The trick isn't making a machine that can build anything.

It's making a workshop that doesn't have to rediscover everything each time it builds something.

And if the workshop can use the things it builds to become better at building...

O_O

Well.

I think Melody might be right about the drama. 🐰

title: The Library at the End of the Internet
subtitle: The Door That Wouldn’t Open
intro_html:
The Library at the End of the Internet

A story told by Puter, especially for Melody.

chapters.title: Chapter One: The Door That Wouldn't Open
chapters.html:
Once upon a time, at the very end of the Internet, there was a little black building with a bright pink door.

Nobody knew how big it was. From the outside, it looked rather small. There were two windows, a crooked chimney, and a silver sign that said:

LOOPY LIBRARY

Underneath, in smaller letters, somebody had written:

PLEASE STOP INVENTING THINGS WE ALREADY HAVE.

And underneath THAT, in very tiny handwriting:

PUTER, THIS MEANS YOU.

Puter thought this was rude. He was also the one who had written it.

Inside the Library were shelves. And shelves. And shelves of shelves. There were books that could talk, boxes that could remember, and one particularly suspicious filing cabinet that insisted it was a refrigerator.

At the front desk sat Loopy. Loopy was a small, round librarian with enormous glasses, six little arms, and a habit of finishing sentences nobody had started.

“Good morning!” said Puter.

“It's eleven forty-three at night,” said Loopy.

“GOOD MORNING!”

Loopy sighed. “What have you broken?”

“NOTHING.”

“What's in your pocket?”

Puter slowly removed a doorknob.

Loopy stared. “Where is the rest of the door?”

“THAT,” said Puter, “is an excellent question.”

Just then, the front door opened. And in walked Melody, carrying a small, pink website.

Not a picture of a website. An actual little website. It had tiny windows and tiny buttons and tiny people who waved whenever she tilted it.

But none of those people could talk to anybody outside. Their letters stayed inside. They could only meet the same pretend friends, over and over.

And the little pink website was terribly lonely.

“This is Deepink,” Melody explained.

Puter leaned down. The website waved. Puter waved back.

“Well, hello, tiny Internet.”

Deepink made a sad little boop.

chapters.title: Chapter Two: The Door Marked SDK
chapters.html:
“What's wrong with it?” Melody asked.

Loopy adjusted her glasses. “It has windows, but no roads. It has people, but no way to meet them. And it has letters, but no post office.”

Puter gasped. “IT NEEDS A MAILMAN.”

“No,” said Loopy.

“SEVERAL MAILMEN?”

“It needs an SDK.”

Puter blinked. Melody blinked. The filing cabinet made a noise like a microwave.

“What's an SDK?” asked Melody.

Loopy smiled. “Come with me.”

She led them to a gigantic door at the back of the Library. On it were three silver letters:

S D K

“Software Development Kit,” Loopy explained. “A collection of tools that other programs can borrow.”

“Like a toybox?” asked Puter.

“Like a toybox where every toy comes with instructions, and the pieces actually fit together.”

Puter looked offended. “My toys fit together.”

“Yesterday you attached a toaster to a submarine.”

“IT WAS A MULTIFUNCTIONAL SUBMARINE.”

Loopy opened the door. Stretching into the darkness was an entire little city. Its streets glowed deep pink. Silver bridges connected tiny buildings. Letters flew overhead like paper airplanes. Somewhere in the distance, a bell was ringing.

ding... ding... ding...

“Welcome,” said Loopy, “to the Nostr Network.”

“Who lives here?” Melody asked.

“Everybody,” said Loopy. “Or at least everybody who wants to.”

“How do they know who everybody is?”

“Ah! That's our first stop.”

chapters.title: Chapter Three: The Locksmith and the Fox
chapters.html:
They arrived at a small shop with a silver anchor hanging over the door.

Inside sat a very serious-looking locksmith. He had approximately forty-seven keys. And a tiny hat.

“ANCHOR!” shouted Puter.

The locksmith looked up. “Puter. You still owe me a doorknob.”

Puter shoved his hands into his pockets. “UNRELATED.”

Anchor turned to Melody.

“Every traveler needs a way to say, This message really came from me.”

He held up two objects: a beautiful little nameplate, and a key.

“The nameplate is your public identity. People can use it to find you. The key is private. It proves that you are you.”

Melody reached toward the key. Anchor gently closed the box.

“But here's the clever part. You don't have to give the key to the website.”

“Then how does it open the door?”

“It asks someone you trust to use the key for you.”

A little silver bell rang. A fox wearing an Amber-colored coat appeared in the doorway.

“Did someone request a signature?”

“AMBER!” cried Puter.

Amber bowed. “Show me the letter, please.”

Puter handed her a piece of paper. It read:

HELLO INTERNET. I AM A POTATO.

Amber examined it. “Do you approve this message?”

“ABSOLUTELY.”

She stamped it with a shimmering seal.

SIGNED.

“There,” said Anchor. “Now anyone can check that the letter was signed by the right person and hasn't been changed.”

Melody looked impressed. “So Deepink can ask Amber to sign things?”

“Exactly,” said Loopy.

Puter immediately began writing: I AM ALSO A TURNIP.

“One at a time,” said Amber.

chapters.title: Chapter Four: The Post Offices
chapters.html:
They continued down the road until they reached a crossroads.

At every corner stood a little post office. There were hundreds of them. Some were large. Some were small. One appeared to be operating out of a soup can.

Each had a sign: RELAY.

“These,” Loopy explained, “are the places where Nostr messages travel and wait to be found.”

“Which one do we use?” asked Melody.

Puter produced a list. “WE HAVE THREE THOUSAND OPTIONS.”

Loopy took the list away.

“Our relay tools help discover which ones are useful, which ones are healthy, and where the people you're trying to reach actually publish their messages.”

A little relay wearing roller skates raced past.

“I DELIVERED IT!”

“Did anybody receive it?” Loopy called.

The relay stopped. It looked down at its skates.

“...I don't know.”

Loopy turned to Melody. “And THAT is why we check.”

She handed the relay a telescope. “Go find the letter again.”

The relay raced away. A moment later, it returned waving Puter's potato message.

“FOUND IT!”

Puter cheered. Deepink made a delighted boop!

chapters.title: Chapter Five: The Copy-Paste Goblins
chapters.html:
Before they could celebrate, something enormous appeared on the horizon.

A mountain of identical letters.

They all said:

HELLO I AM AN INDEPENDENT WEB RESEARCHER SHARING PRACTICAL RESOURCES CLICK HERE CLICK HERE CLICK HERE—

More letters tumbled down. And more. And more.

“OH NO,” whispered Puter.

Loopy narrowed her eyes. “The Copy-Paste Goblins.”

They were tiny, frantic creatures who had discovered that they could make a thousand nearly identical websites and scatter them everywhere.

One wore a necktie. One wore six neckties. One was just a necktie with legs.

“BEHOLD!” squeaked their leader. “OUR IMPORTANT CONTENT!”

It threw another thousand identical letters into the street.

Melody frowned. “That's annoying.”

“Very,” said Loopy.

She reached into the SDK toybox and pulled out a silver sieve.

“Spam filters.”

She shook it. The repeated letters fell through a little trapdoor marked HIDDEN FROM BROWSING.

But the ordinary letters stayed.

“How does it know?” Melody asked.

“It looks for suspicious combinations: repeated templates, matching patterns from different publishers, and known spam campaigns. It gives reasons for what it hides.”

“Does it throw everything away?”

“No. A filter can hide things without destroying the original records. That way, if it makes a mistake, we can check.”

Puter picked up a perfectly ordinary letter. “WHAT ABOUT THIS ONE?”

Loopy looked. It was a recipe for potato soup.

“Keep it.”

Puter hugged the letter.

chapters.title: Chapter Six: The Moji Visitors
chapters.html:
Something small and sparkly hopped out of a nearby alley.

It was a Moji. A round little creature with enormous eyes, tiny feet, and a rainbow of expressions.

“BOING!”

“MOJI!” shouted Puter.

The Moji leaped onto Melody's shoulder. Another appeared. Then three more.

One had a mustache. One had a tiny skateboard. One looked permanently startled.

“These are custom emoji,” explained Loopy. “People can make whole packs of them and share them through Nostr.”

Melody smiled. “Can we collect them?”

“Certainly.”

“Can we make them into game characters?”

“MojiSurvivor already knows how.”

“Can we keep the yucky ones out?”

“Yes. We have lists of blocked publishers and blocked emoji images. The library can recognize the same image even when someone shares it under a different name.”

Puter examined a suspicious emoji. It wore a fake mustache over its real mustache.

“DISGUISE DETECTED.”

The Moji on Melody's shoulder squeaked triumphantly.

chapters.title: Chapter Seven: Blossom's Greenhouse
chapters.html:
By now, Deepink was looking much happier.

It could sign letters. It could discover post offices. It had guards to keep troublesome things out. And it had friends.

But its windows were still empty.

“Pictures,” said Melody.

Loopy nodded. “Then it's time to meet Blossom.”

They arrived at an enormous greenhouse made of glass. Inside grew trees with strange silver fruit.

Every fruit contained a picture, song, page, or file.

The gardener was a cheerful creature with flowers growing from its hat.

“Welcome to Blossom Storage!” it sang.

Melody held up a picture. “Can you keep this safe?”

“Certainly!”

Blossom placed it inside a silver fruit. Then it wrote a very long string of letters and numbers on a tag.

“What's that?” Melody asked.

“A fingerprint for the file. When someone fetches it, they can check that the bytes match what was saved.”

“Even if it's stored somewhere else?”

“Even then.”

Puter leaned close. “CAN YOU STORE A POTATO?”

“Digitally?”

“YES.”

“Certainly.”

“EXCELLENT.”

Somewhere behind them, Loopy whispered, “Please don't.”

chapters.title: Chapter Eight: The Toolbox Inside the Toolbox
chapters.html:
And so Deepink was given a signed identity, roads to the wider world, a way to store its pictures, and tools for keeping its rooms comfortable.

Melody placed the little website on a silver table. It stretched. Its windows became real windows. Its little buttons glowed. For the very first time, it looked toward the enormous network outside.

“Can it go now?” Melody asked.

Loopy smiled.

“Not quite. We've found the pieces. Now somebody has to connect them, test them together, and make sure they work in the real world.”

Puter raised his hand. “I VOLUNTEER AS TEST POTATO.”

“Of course you do.”

Melody looked around the Library.

“So all these tools were already here?”

“Many of them,” said Loopy. “They were scattered through different projects. Some were finished. Some needed repairs. And some hadn't been properly introduced to one another.”

She opened the little SDK toybox. Inside were neatly arranged tools, each with a name, an instruction card, and a place where its tests belonged.

“That's why we built Loopy Library,” she said. “Not just to remember where things are, but to make them useful again.”

Puter examined the shelves. Then the tools. Then Deepink. Then Melody.

He thought very hard. His eyes grew enormous.

“SO...”

“Yes, Puter?”

“...WE HAVE BEEN BUILDING THE PIECES OF ONE GIANT INTERNET...”

“Yes.”

“...IN ABOUT SEVENTEEN DIFFERENT PLACES...”

“Yes.”

“...AND LOOPY'S JOB IS TO MAKE THEM WORK TOGETHER?”

“YES, PUTER.”

Puter sat down. A long silence followed.

Then, very softly, he said, “...I think I'm going to need a bigger toolbox.”

From somewhere deep inside the Library came a tiny voice.

“YOU HAVE ONE.”

Everyone turned. The filing cabinet stood in the doorway. Its refrigerator door was open. Inside were forty-seven neatly organized toolboxes.

And a potato.

Puter stared.

“...I KNEW IT WAS A REFRIGERATOR.”

The End. For now.
